questions.stem: A 34 year old chef has a 3 day history of worsening throbbing pain next to his anus. He now has to sit on one buttock and has felt shivery. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. There is a hot, red, fluctuant swelling 2 cm from the anal verge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute, throbbing and fluctuant = an abscess (an acute pus collection). Why not Thrombosed external haemorrhoid? A tense bluish lump, painful but not hot, fluctuant or febrile.

clues: throbbing pain next to his anus
fluctuant swelling 2 cm from the anal verge
steps.x: Acute throbbing pain, a fluctuant red swelling by the anus and fever.

elim: A tense bluish lump, painful but not hot, fluctuant or febrile.
Lies in the natal cleft over the sacrum, not beside the anal verge.
Itching without a fluctuant swelling or fever.
A soft vascular lump at the verge without fever or fluctuance.

steps.x: **A. Perianal abscess.** Acute, throbbing and fluctuant = an abscess (an acute pus collection).

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has had intermittent staining of her underwear with pus and a little blood for 7 months. The skin beside her anus itches. A year ago she had a painful perianal swelling that burst on its own. There is a small opening on the perianal skin at 4 o'clock that discharges pus when pressed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A chronic discharging external opening after an abscess = fistula (a chronic abnormal tract). Why not Anal fissure? Pain on defecation and bright red blood, no external opening discharging pus.

clues: staining of her underwear with pus
small opening on the perianal skin
steps.x: Chronic discharge, an external opening near the anus, previous abscess that burst.

elim: Pain on defecation and bright red blood, no external opening discharging pus.
Multiple nodules and sinuses in the axillae and groin, not a single tract after an abscess.
An acute painful fluctuant collection; this is a chronic discharging tract.
Itching alone, with no discharging opening.

steps.x: **B. Anal fistula.** A chronic discharging external opening after an abscess = fistula (a chronic abnormal tract).

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a perianal abscess drained. He is otherwise well, with no diabetes, no bowel symptoms and no previous perianal problems. He takes no regular medicines and has not lost weight. At follow-up in clinic the wound is healing well and he asks what caused it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Most perianal abscesses and fistulas come from infected anal glands. Why not Crohn's disease? Suspect with recurrent disease, diarrhoea and weight loss, none of which he has.

steps.x: First abscess, no risk factors, no bowel symptoms.

elim: Suspect with recurrent disease, diarrhoea and weight loss, none of which he has.
Causes pain on defecation and a posterior tear, not an abscess.
Causes proctitis, not the usual cause of a perianal abscess.
A rare cause, not the common one in a well young man.

steps.x: **C. Cryptoglandular infection.** Most perianal abscesses and fistulas come from infected anal glands.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has her third perianal abscess in a year and a discharging opening beside the anus. She has had loose stools up to 6 times a day for 4 months and has lost 6 kg. Her CRP is 48 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her perianal disease?
questions.e: Recurrent fistula or sepsis + diarrhoea + weight loss = think Crohn's. Why not Small bowel lymphoma? Rare, and does not typically cause recurrent perianal fistulas.

clues: third perianal abscess in a year
steps.x: Recurrent abscesses and a fistula plus diarrhoea, weight loss and raised CRP.

elim: Rare, and does not typically cause recurrent perianal fistulas.
No weight loss or raised CRP, and no fistulas.
Mucosal disease limited to the colon; perianal fistulas are not typical.
Raises abscess risk but does not cause diarrhoea and weight loss.

steps.x: **A. Crohn's disease.** Recurrent fistula or sepsis + diarrhoea + weight loss = think Crohn's.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 4 day history of perianal pain and fever. He has had type 2 diabetes for 15 years. His temperature is 38.4°C. There is a tender fluctuant perianal swelling. His HbA1c is 86 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which factor most increases his risk of this condition?
questions.e: Diabetes impairs immunity and wound healing, so abscesses form and heal slowly. Why not Age over 60? Not itself the main risk; his poorly controlled diabetes is.

steps.x: Long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes.

elim: Not itself the main risk; his poorly controlled diabetes is.
Linked to fissures and haemorrhoids, not abscesses.
A minor association compared with diabetes.
Not a risk factor for perianal sepsis.

steps.x: **C. Long-standing diabetes mellitus.** Diabetes impairs immunity and wound healing, so abscesses form and heal slowly.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had a perianal abscess 5 months ago, treated by his GP with oral antibiotics only. The swelling settled but he now has a small opening beside the anus that leaks pus intermittently onto his underwear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication he has developed?
questions.e: An undrained or persistent abscess can track and form a fistula. Why not Anal stenosis? Causes difficult, narrow stools, not a discharging opening.

clues: small opening beside the anus that leaks pus
steps.x: Abscess not drained, then a chronic discharging opening.

elim: Causes difficult, narrow stools, not a discharging opening.
Loss of control, not pus from an opening beside the anus.
Rapidly spreading necrotising infection with severe illness, not a chronic leak.
In the natal cleft, unrelated to an anal abscess.

steps.x: **C. Fistula-in-ano.** An undrained or persistent abscess can track and form a fistula.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 3 day history of perianal pain. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg. She has had type 2 diabetes for 10 years. She has throbbing pain beside the anus, cannot sit comfortably and has felt unwell for 2 days.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Tender fluctuant swelling with surrounding erythema
questions.e: An abscess is tender, fluctuant and red, often with fever; spreading erythema means cellulitis too. Why not Bluish thrombosed vein? Seen in a thrombosed haemorrhoid, not an abscess.

steps.x: Acute throbbing perianal pain, fever, tachycardia and difficulty sitting.

elim: Seen in a thrombosed haemorrhoid, not an abscess.
Suggests necrotising infection, which this picture does not show.
Suggests primary syphilis or malignancy.
A sentinel tag goes with a chronic fissure.

steps.x: **E. Tender fluctuant swelling with surrounding erythema.** An abscess is tender, fluctuant and red, often with fever; spreading erythema means cellulitis too.

questions.stem: A 37 year old lorry driver has had recurrent perianal swellings that burst every few months for 2 years. Between episodes there is intermittent pus and local irritation around the anus, and he wears a pad in his underwear. He has no bowel symptoms or weight loss. There is a firm cord palpable beneath the perianal skin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anus
questions.e: Recurrent abscesses + intermittent pus = a chronic fistula tract. Why not Squamous cell carcinoma of the anus? Usually an indurated mass or ulcer with bleeding, not repeated bursting swellings.

steps.x: Recurrent abscesses with intermittent pus between them.

elim: Usually an indurated mass or ulcer with bleeding, not repeated bursting swellings.
Bleeding and prolapse, not repeated pus discharge.
Cauliflower-like lesions, no pus.
Over the sacrum in the natal cleft, not around the anus.

steps.x: **A. Anal fistula.** Recurrent abscesses + intermittent pus = a chronic fistula tract.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman takes methotrexate and prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis. She has a 5 day history of perianal pain and a tender, fluctuant swelling. Her surgeon says her drug history makes this more likely and slower to heal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason?
o: Immunosuppression impairing local defence and wound healing
Rheumatoid vasculitis of the anal canal
questions.e: Immunosuppression and diabetes both impair local immunity and healing. Why not Thrombocytopenia from methotrexate? Causes bleeding, not abscesses.

steps.x: Immunosuppressants and slow healing.

elim: Causes bleeding, not abscesses.
Constipation is not the link to abscess formation.
Not a recognised cause of perianal abscess.
Steroids do not cause haemorrhoids.

steps.x: **A. Immunosuppression impairing local defence and wound healing.** Immunosuppression and diabetes both impair local immunity and healing.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has a 48 hour history of severe constant pain beside the anus, worse on coughing and sitting. He has no discharge. There is a tender, warm, fluctuant lump at 7 o'clock just outside the anal verge.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Abscess = acute; fistula = chronic. Why not Anal fistula? A chronic discharging tract; this is a 2 day acute collection.

steps.x: 48 hours, severe pain, warm fluctuant lump.

elim: A chronic discharging tract; this is a 2 day acute collection.
Vague rectal ache without a lump.
Sudden painful bluish lump, not warm and fluctuant.
Mucosa protruding through the anus, usually painless.

steps.x: **C. Perianal abscess.** Abscess = acute; fistula = chronic.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 2 day history of throbbing perianal pain. Her temperature is 37.9°C. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. There is an obvious tender fluctuant swelling beside the anus. She has no previous perianal disease, no bowel symptoms and no diabetes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: A simple perianal abscess is diagnosed clinically. Why not CT abdomen and pelvis? Not needed for an obvious superficial abscess.

steps.x: Obvious fluctuant swelling, first episode.

elim: Not needed for an obvious superficial abscess.
For complex or unclear disease, not a typical abscess.
Examines the bowel lumen, not a perianal collection.
For deep, unclear, recurrent or complex disease.

steps.x: **A. Clinical history and examination.** A simple perianal abscess is diagnosed clinically.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has deep rectal pain and fever for 5 days. His temperature is 38.8°C. Perianal skin looks normal, but rectal examination shows tenderness and fullness high on the left side. His white cell count is 17 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Deep or unclear perianal sepsis (e.g. supralevator) needs MRI pelvis. Why not Abdominal X-ray? Cannot show a pelvic collection.

clues: fullness high on the left side
steps.x: Deep pain, fever, normal skin, high fullness on PR: a deep collection.

elim: Cannot show a pelvic collection.
Will not locate or define the collection.
Looks at the mucosa, not a collection outside the bowel wall.
Screens for bowel inflammation, not a deep abscess.

steps.x: **E. MRI pelvis.** Deep or unclear perianal sepsis (e.g. supralevator) needs MRI pelvis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has had a discharging perianal opening for a year after an abscess. There is a single external opening at 7 o'clock. She has no bowel symptoms. The colorectal surgeon plans definitive treatment and wants to define the tract and its internal opening.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate assessment?
o: MRI pelvis and examination under anaesthesia
questions.e: Fistula: MRI pelvis + EUA is the gold-standard combination. Why not Barium enema? Shows the colon lumen, not a fistula tract.

clues: discharging perianal opening for a year
define the tract and its internal opening
steps.x: A fistula, and the surgeon needs the tract mapped.

elim: Shows the colon lumen, not a fistula tract.
Poor at defining tracts relative to the sphincters.
Outdated and less accurate than MRI with EUA.
Cannot define the whole tract.

steps.x: **D. MRI pelvis and examination under anaesthesia.** Fistula: MRI pelvis + EUA is the gold-standard combination.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has had four perianal abscesses in 2 years, each drained. He now has two external openings with intermittent pus. He has no bowel symptoms and is otherwise well. Examination in clinic is painful and cannot show where the tracts run. The surgeon suspects a complex tract.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
questions.e: Recurrent or complex perianal disease is imaged with MRI pelvis. Why not CT colonography? Looks for colonic polyps and cancer.

steps.x: Recurrent abscesses, two openings, complex tract.

elim: Looks for colonic polyps and cancer.
Cannot show soft tissue tracts.
Cannot see the anal sphincter complex well.
Irrelevant to a perianal tract.

steps.x: **B. MRI pelvis.** Recurrent or complex perianal disease is imaged with MRI pelvis.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has a 3 day history of perianal pain. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm. There is a 3 cm tender fluctuant swelling beside the anus with no surrounding redness. He is otherwise well, with no diabetes or immunosuppression.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Incision and drainage is the initial and definitive treatment of a perianal abscess. Why not Fistulotomy? Treats a fistula, not an acute abscess.

steps.x: Fluctuant abscess, no cellulitis, well.

elim: Treats a fistula, not an acute abscess.
Pus must be drained; delay risks spread and a fistula.
For fistulas, not a simple acute abscess.
Treats an anal fissure.

steps.x: **C. Incision and drainage.** Incision and drainage is the initial and definitive treatment of a perianal abscess.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes has a perianal abscess with redness and induration spreading 6 cm across the buttock. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Drain every abscess; add antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic infection. Why not Incision and drainage alone? Cellulitis and systemic features mean antibiotics are also needed.

steps.x: Spreading cellulitis and systemic signs.

elim: Cellulitis and systemic features mean antibiotics are also needed.
The pus must still be drained.
She is septic; drainage should not wait.
Fistula treatment, not for an acute abscess.

steps.x: **B. Incision and drainage with antibiotics.** Drain every abscess; add antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic infection.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has had a discharging opening beside her anus for 9 months. She has had three vaginal deliveries. MRI pelvis shows a tract crossing a large part of the external sphincter. She is worried about incontinence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Fistulas need colorectal surgery: fistulotomy for low tracts, seton when sphincter is at risk. Why not Incision and drainage? For an acute abscess, not a chronic tract.

clues: tract crossing a large part of the external sphincter
steps.x: Fistula crossing much of the sphincter, worry about continence.

elim: For an acute abscess, not a chronic tract.
Do not cure a fistula.
Treats a fissure and would risk incontinence.
Has no role in a fistula.

steps.x: **C. Seton placement.** Fistulas need colorectal surgery: fistulotomy for low tracts, seton when sphincter is at risk.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man is seen by his GP with a 6 month history of discharge from an opening beside his anus. He now has a new painful fluctuant swelling next to the opening and a temperature of 38.0°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start a 6 week course of antibiotics
questions.e: A fistula with a perianal abscess is referred to general surgery. Why not Prescribe topical glyceryl trinitrate? Treats an anal fissure.

clues: discharge from an opening beside his anus
steps.x: Known fistula with a new abscess and fever.

elim: Treats an anal fissure.
Untreated sepsis will worsen.
Surgery is needed to drain the abscess and treat the tract.
Antibiotics alone do not drain pus or close a fistula.

steps.x: **D. Refer to general surgery.** A fistula with a perianal abscess is referred to general surgery.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has a low anal fistula that involves only a small amount of the internal sphincter on MRI pelvis and examination under anaesthesia. He has normal continence and no Crohn's disease. He has had intermittent discharge for 8 months and wants it cured.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Low simple fistulas are laid open (fistulotomy) by a colorectal surgeon. Why not Botulinum toxin injection? Treats a fissure.

steps.x: A low, simple fistula with normal continence.

elim: Treats a fissure.
For an acute abscess.
Does not cure a fistula.
Treats haemorrhoids.

steps.x: **B. Fistulotomy.** Low simple fistulas are laid open (fistulotomy) by a colorectal surgeon.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has a perianal abscess drained. She has no bowel symptoms and is not diabetic. The pus was in the ischiorectal space. The registrar explains to a student where these infections usually start, before they spread into the spaces around the anal sphincters.
questions.q: Which is the most likely origin of the infection?
o: Hair follicles in the natal cleft
Obstructed anal glands at the dentate line
questions.e: Cryptoglandular: anal crypt glands at the dentate line block and become infected. Why not Haemorrhoidal venous plexus? Thrombosis here causes haemorrhoids, not abscesses.

steps.x: Where perianal infections start.

elim: Thrombosis here causes haemorrhoids, not abscesses.
Origin of pilonidal disease.
Not the source of perianal sepsis.
Inguinal nodes do not form perianal abscesses.

steps.x: **E. Obstructed anal glands at the dentate line.** Cryptoglandular: anal crypt glands at the dentate line block and become infected.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has an anal fistula with an external opening at 5 o'clock, 4 cm from the anal verge, posterior to a line drawn across the anus. The surgeon predicts the tract will curve to an internal opening in the posterior midline.
questions.q: Which principle is the surgeon using?
questions.e: Goodsall's rule predicts the course and internal opening of a fistula from the external opening. Why not Courvoisier's law? Relates a palpable gallbladder to jaundice.

clues: posterior to a line drawn across the anus
steps.x: External opening position used to predict the internal opening.

elim: Relates a palpable gallbladder to jaundice.
About joint innervation.
Stages colorectal cancer.
Explains venous thrombosis.

steps.x: **C. Goodsall's rule.** Goodsall's rule predicts the course and internal opening of a fistula from the external opening.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman had a perianal abscess that was only partly drained. Months later she has intermittent pus on her underwear. At examination under anaesthesia an epithelium-lined tract is found running from the anal canal to the perianal skin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this tract?
o: A persistent abscess tracking and epithelialising
Congenital failure of the anal membrane
Malignant invasion of the anal canal
questions.e: Inadequately drained infection tracks and epithelialises into a fistula. Why not Congenital failure of the anal membrane? Causes anorectal malformations in infants.

steps.x: Partly drained abscess, then a lined tract from canal to skin.

elim: Causes anorectal malformations in infants.
Not how a fistula forms.
Nothing suggests cancer.
Mechanism of haemorrhoids.

steps.x: **A. A persistent abscess tracking and epithelialising.** Inadequately drained infection tracks and epithelialises into a fistula.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with ileocolonic Crohn's disease develops a perianal abscess and then a fistula to the perianal skin. A student asks why Crohn's disease, but not ulcerative colitis, so often causes fistulas.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Crypt abscesses confined to the mucosa
Transmural inflammation of the bowel wall
questions.e: Crohn's is full-thickness (transmural), so tracts can form through the wall. Why not Crypt abscesses confined to the mucosa? Mucosal disease is the pattern in ulcerative colitis.

steps.x: Crohn's vs UC: depth of inflammation.

elim: Mucosal disease is the pattern in ulcerative colitis.
Not the reason tracts form.
Linked to fissures, not fistulas.
Results from terminal ileal disease, not fistulas.

steps.x: **D. Transmural inflammation of the bowel wall.** Crohn's is full-thickness (transmural), so tracts can form through the wall.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 30 years had a perianal abscess drained 6 weeks ago. The wound is still open and slow to heal despite regular dressings by the district nurse. He has no bowel symptoms. His HbA1c is 92 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for the slow healing?
o: Poor immune defence and wound healing from diabetes
questions.e: Diabetes impairs immunity and healing, raising risk and delaying resolution. Why not Anal sphincter spasm? Delays fissure healing, not abscess wounds.

steps.x: Long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes and a slow wound.

elim: Delays fissure healing, not abscess wounds.
No evidence given.
No mass or features of cancer.
Not the main reason in poorly controlled diabetes.

steps.x: **E. Poor immune defence and wound healing from diabetes.** Diabetes impairs immunity and healing, raising risk and delaying resolution.
